prompt: Before connecting, the computer turns 'shop.example.com' into a numeric address.
why: Names are for people; computers need IP addresses. Looking up the address for a name is DNS.
trap: The request comes after; this is finding where to send it.

prompt: The site vanished because the company forgot to renew its domain name.
tells: forgot to renew its domain name
why: Without the domain, the name no longer points to the server's address. That's DNS.
trap: Nothing crashed; the name stopped resolving.

prompt: After moving to a new server, some visitors still reached the old one for a few hours until the name updated everywhere.
why: DNS answers are cached, so a changed address takes time to spread. That's DNS.
trap: Caching plays a part, but it's the name-to-address record that changed.

prompt: The browser shows 'server not found' because the name can't be matched to an address.
tells: the name can't be matched to an address
why: Matching a name to an address failed, so no connection was made. That's a DNS problem.
trap: A 404 comes from a server; here no server was reached at all.

prompt: Typing 'gooogle.com' takes you to a different site because that name points somewhere else.
why: Each domain name points to its own address. A different name means a different server. That's DNS.
trap: Encryption doesn't decide where you go; the name lookup does.

prompt: Typing the server's number directly works even though the name doesn't.
tells: Typing the server's number directly works
why: If the address works but the name doesn't, the name lookup is broken. That's DNS.
trap: The server is fine; only the name-to-address step fails.
